uke-1.title: Unit Introduction and Kinematics Context
uke-1.summary: Week 1 establishes the course's working methods and shows why robots must be described with coordinate frames, transformations and kinematic chains. The first half of EGB339 goes from mathematical pose description to controlling the Dobot; the second half continues to robot vision.
uke-1.body:
> [!abstract] TL;DR
> Week 1 establishes the course's working methods and shows why robots must be described with coordinate frames, transformations and kinematic chains. The first half of EGB339 goes from mathematical pose description to controlling the Dobot; the second half continues to robot vision.

## What you need to know

- EGB339 combines mathematics and Python: matrix operations, geometry, trigonometry and code are used together in the assessments.
- A robot can be understood as a chain of frames and joints. A known transformation from `{A}` to `{B}` and from `{B}` to `{C}` can be composed into a transformation from `{A}` to `{C}`.
- The Gradescope tasks expect general Python functions that compute answers from the function arguments, not hardcoded example values.
- Assessment code must be the student's own work and must not be published publicly. The course allows GenAI as learning and development support, but understanding is also checked in the viva.
## Key concepts

- [Reference frames](/egb339/temaer/reference-frames)
- [Kinematic chains and joints](/egb339/temaer/kinematic-chains-and-joints)
- [Pose graphs](/egb339/temaer/pose-graphs)
- [Forward kinematics](/egb339/temaer/forward-kinematics)

## Tools and systems

- [Dobot Magician](/egb339/temaer/dobot-magician)
- [CoppeliaSim](/egb339/temaer/coppeliasim)

## Connection to assessment

- Problem-solving tasks use automatic tests of Python functions.
- The applied project requires that robot kinematics both works in code and can be explained orally.

## Open questions

- Which parts of the assessment rules are course-specific, and which come from QUT's general policy?
- Which concrete joint and frame definitions are used later for the Dobot model?

uke-2.title: Linear Algebra and 2D Pose
uke-2.summary: Week 2 reviews Python and linear algebra before position and orientation are combined in 2D. SO(2) describes pure rotation; SE(2) adds translation through homogeneous coordinates.
uke-2.body:
> [!abstract] TL;DR
> Week 2 reviews Python and linear algebra before position and orientation are combined in 2D. `SO(2)` describes pure rotation; `SE(2)` adds translation through homogeneous coordinates.

## What you need to know

- Matrix multiplication is repeated dot products. The dimensions must match, and the order can change the result.
- A 2D rotation with angle `θ` is described by `R = [[cos θ, -sin θ], [sin θ, cos θ]]`.
- A rotation matrix is orthogonal and has determinant `+1`; therefore the inverse equals the transpose.
- The notation must be read as frames: a transformation describing `{B}` relative to `{A}` is used to express a point from `{B}` in `{A}`. The opposite direction requires the inverse.
- A 2D pose is collected in a `3×3` homogeneous `SE(2)` matrix, and the point is extended with a final homogeneous coordinate equal to `1`.
## Key concepts

- [Linear algebra for robotics](/egb339/temaer/linear-algebra-for-robotics)
- [Reference frames](/egb339/temaer/reference-frames)
- [SO(2) rotation matrices](/egb339/temaer/so-2-rotation-matrices)
- [SE(2) homogeneous transformations](/egb339/temaer/se-2-homogeneous-transformations)

## Connection to assessment

- Functions should work for general angles, vectors and matrices.
- Floating-point numbers should be compared with tolerance, for example `np.isclose` and `np.allclose`, not always with exact `==`.
- [Assessment 1.1 - Position and orientation in 2D](/egb339/vurderinger/assessment-1-1-position-and-orientation-in-2d) applies the whole week-2 chain: construct and validate `SO(2)`, choose the correct transformation direction, and then extend to `SE(2)`.
- [Assessment 1.0 - Warmup to Gradescope](/egb339/vurderinger/assessment-1-0-warmup-to-gradescope) provides an optional check of the Python, NumPy and matrix foundation before this chain is used in assessed tasks.

## Open questions

- Which superscript/subscript convention is explicitly expected in exam answers?

uke-3.title: NumPy and 3D Pose
uke-3.summary: Week 3 extends the 2D model to three dimensions. SO(3) describes orientation, SE(3) describes full pose, and pose graphs determine which transformations must be multiplied to connect distant frames. NumPy is the computation tool.
uke-3.body:
> [!abstract] TL;DR
> Week 3 extends the 2D model to three dimensions. `SO(3)` describes orientation, `SE(3)` describes full pose, and pose graphs determine which transformations must be multiplied to connect distant frames. NumPy is the computation tool.

## What you need to know

- 3D has its own standard rotations about the x-, y- and z-axes. All valid `SO(3)` matrices are orthogonal and have determinant `+1`.
- Rotations about different 3D axes are not commutative. The wording “new/local axis” versus “old/global axis” determines on which side the next rotation is multiplied.
- An `SE(3)` matrix has a `3×3` rotation block, a `3×1` translation vector and bottom row `[0, 0, 0, 1]`.
- Pose graphs let us find an indirect transformation by following a connected chain of frames and matching the indices.
- In NumPy, `@` means matrix multiplication. `*` means element-wise multiplication, and broadcasting can give a runnable but mathematically wrong result if the shapes are not checked.
## Key concepts

- [NumPy arrays and matrix operations](/egb339/temaer/numpy-arrays-and-matrix-operations)
- [SO(3) rotation matrices](/egb339/temaer/so-3-rotation-matrices)
- [SE(3) homogeneous transformations](/egb339/temaer/se-3-homogeneous-transformations)
- [Rotation composition in 3D](/egb339/temaer/rotation-composition-in-3d)
- [Pose graphs](/egb339/temaer/pose-graphs)

## Connection to assessment

- Use `np.array`, check `.shape`, and use `@` when the function should multiply matrices or transform vectors.
- Large transformation products can be kept symbolic when the task allows it, but the factors and the order must be unambiguous.

## Open questions

- Do all tasks use the same convention for new and old rotation axes, or must it be derived from each task text?

uke-4.title: Forward Kinematics
uke-4.summary: Forward kinematics finds the robot's end-effector pose from joint values and geometry. The robot arm is divided into an ordered chain where each joint gives a rotation or prismatic displacement, and each link gives a translation.
uke-4.body:
> [!abstract] TL;DR
> Forward kinematics finds the robot's end-effector pose from joint values and geometry. The robot arm is divided into an ordered chain where each joint gives a rotation or prismatic displacement, and each link gives a translation.

## What you need to know

- Forward kinematics is a pose graph where the transformations depend on joint angles or prismatic joint lengths.
- A robust working method is: rotate at joint 1, translate along link 1, rotate at joint 2, translate along link 2, and continue until the end effector.
- Coordinate frames can be chosen in several valid ways. The choice changes the individual factors, but not the final pose when all fixed offsets are handled consistently.
- Rotation and translation can be combined in one transformation, but the translation vector is expressed in a specific frame. The multiplication order therefore determines whether the motion happens along original or rotated axes.
- The practical uses CoppeliaSim to compare the computed Dobot position with the robot model.
## Key concepts

- [Kinematic chains and joints](/egb339/temaer/kinematic-chains-and-joints)
- [Pose graphs](/egb339/temaer/pose-graphs)
- [Forward kinematics](/egb339/temaer/forward-kinematics)
- [Joint-angle mapping](/egb339/temaer/joint-angle-mapping)

## Tools and systems

- [Dobot Magician](/egb339/temaer/dobot-magician)
- [CoppeliaSim](/egb339/temaer/coppeliasim)

## Connection to assessment

- Draw all frames and write the transformation product before implementing.
- Keep length units consistent; the practical shows millimetres that are converted to metres.
- Verify both a known home configuration and several non-trivial joint angles.

## Open questions

- Which exact Dobot dimensions and zero angles apply in Assessment 1.3 compared with the practical model?

uke-5.title: Inverse Kinematics
uke-5.summary: Inverse kinematics goes the opposite way of forward kinematics: from a desired end-effector position to joint values. The week focuses on geometric solution, trigonometric branch selection, atan2, workspace and several possible robot configurations.
uke-5.body:
> [!abstract] TL;DR
> Inverse kinematics goes the opposite way of forward kinematics: from a desired end-effector position to joint values. The week focuses on geometric solution, trigonometric branch selection, `atan2`, workspace and several possible robot configurations.

## What you need to know

- Three main methods are presented: numerical approximation, algebraic rearrangement of FK and geometric analysis.
- Geometric IK solves the robot geometry as triangles with angle rules, the sine/cosine rule and auxiliary geometry.
- The same target point can give several solutions, especially elbow up and elbow down. Each geometric branch must be handled explicitly.
- A point outside the robot's workspace has no real solution. An implementation must therefore check the reach and the domain of the inverse trigonometric functions.
- `np.atan2(o, a)` preserves the signs of both the opposite and adjacent components and selects the correct quadrant; `np.atan(o/a)` can lose this information. There is no corresponding `asin2` or `acos2`.
## Key concepts

- [Inverse kinematics](/egb339/temaer/inverse-kinematics)
- [atan2 and inverse trigonometry](/egb339/temaer/atan2-and-inverse-trigonometry)
- [Robot workspace and IK solution branches](/egb339/temaer/robot-workspace-and-ik-solution-branches)
- [Forward kinematics](/egb339/temaer/forward-kinematics)

## Connection to assessment

- Draw and label the geometry before coding the equations.
- Use `atan2` where both the x- and y-components are known.
- Test positive and negative quadrants, boundary points and unreachable targets.
- Check the IK result by sending the joint values back through FK.

## Open questions

- Which of the possible IK branches should the Dobot API prioritise when several are physically valid?
- Which mechanical joint limits narrow the mathematical workspace?

uke-6.title: Robot Jacobian
uke-6.summary: The Jacobian matrix is the derivative of forward kinematics and connects joint velocities to end-effector velocity. It is built from partial derivatives, depends on the robot's current configuration and can be used locally to compute small changes in joint or Cartesian coordinates.
uke-6.body:
> [!abstract] TL;DR
> The Jacobian matrix is the derivative of [Forward kinematics](/egb339/temaer/forward-kinematics) and connects joint velocities to end-effector velocity. It is built from partial derivatives, depends on the robot's current configuration and can be used locally to compute small changes in joint or Cartesian coordinates.

## What you need to know

- Forward kinematics is described as a vector function `p = FK(q)`. The Jacobian `J(q)` is the matrix of all partial derivatives `∂pᵢ/∂qⱼ`.
- The end-effector velocity is obtained from the joint velocity with `ṗ = J(q)q̇`. Joint velocities for revolute joints must be expressed in radians per second.
- The Jacobian must be evaluated in the current joint configuration; the same joint velocity can therefore give different Cartesian velocity in different poses.
- If the Jacobian is invertible, a desired Cartesian velocity can be converted to joint velocity with `q̇ = J(q)⁻¹ṗ`. A singular Jacobian has no ordinary inverse.
- For short time steps, `Δp ≈ J(q)Δq` and `Δq ≈ J(q)⁻¹Δp` give a local linear approximation of the non-linear robot motion.
- The Jacobian can be computed by hand or symbolically in SymPy by defining the FK expressions, using `.jacobian()` and substituting current values with `.subs()`.
- The board, the solution sheet and the lecture script show the same workflow from explicit FK via partial differentiation to a numerically evaluated Jacobian.
## Key concepts

- [Partial derivatives for robotics](/egb339/temaer/partial-derivatives-for-robotics)
- [Robot Jacobian](/egb339/temaer/robot-jacobian)
- [Differential kinematics and local linearisation](/egb339/temaer/differential-kinematics-and-local-linearisation)
- [Forward kinematics](/egb339/temaer/forward-kinematics)

## Connection to assessment

- Write FK as explicit position equations before the Jacobian is derived.
- Check the dimensions: a position vector with `m` components and `n` joints gives an `m×n` Jacobian.
- Always evaluate `J(q)` in the configuration the calculation applies to.
- Compare the linear `Δp` approximation with the new position from full FK.
- Test whether the Jacobian is singular before an ordinary matrix inverse is used.

## Open questions

- How is a non-square or nearly singular Jacobian handled when an ordinary inverse cannot be used?
- How small must the time step be before the local linearisation is sufficiently accurate for the robot motion in question?

uke-7.title: Motion Planning
uke-7.summary: Motion planning chooses how the robot moves between two poses. Cartesian interpolation makes a straight end-effector path but requires IK at every waypoint; joint interpolation is simpler in joint space but generally produces a curved Cartesian path. Velocity profiles control timing, while point-to-segment distance provides a basic clearance test.
uke-7.body:
> [!abstract] TL;DR
> Motion planning chooses how the robot moves between two poses. Cartesian interpolation makes a straight end-effector path but requires IK at every waypoint; joint interpolation is simpler in joint space but generally produces a curved Cartesian path. Velocity profiles control timing, while point-to-segment distance provides a basic clearance test.

## What you need to know

- For `n` Cartesian waypoints, waypoint `i` can be generated as `pᵢ = pₛ + (pₑ-pₛ)i/(n-1)`, followed by IK at every point. This keeps the end-effector on the straight line between its endpoints.
- Joint interpolation first finds endpoint joint configurations, interpolates the joint angles, and then uses FK. Its Cartesian path is normally curved.
- A trapezoidal velocity profile separates acceleration, constant-speed travel and deceleration. Travel distance is the area under the velocity curve, while acceleration is the curve's slope.
- Obstacle clearance can be estimated by treating links as line segments, projecting obstacle points onto them and measuring the closest distance.
## Key concepts

- [Robot motion interpolation](/egb339/temaer/robot-motion-interpolation)
- [Trapezoidal motion profiles](/egb339/temaer/trapezoidal-motion-profiles)
- [Point-to-segment distance and obstacle clearance](/egb339/temaer/point-to-segment-distance-and-obstacle-clearance)
- [Inverse kinematics](/egb339/temaer/inverse-kinematics)
- [Forward kinematics](/egb339/temaer/forward-kinematics)

## Connection to assessment

- Explain why Cartesian interpolation calls IK repeatedly, while joint interpolation calls IK only for the endpoints.
- Plot or inspect the FK result of an interpolated joint path before assuming it is collision-free.
- Keep path geometry and time parametrisation separate: waypoints describe where to move; the velocity profile describes when.
- Test link clearance throughout the path, not only at the starting and ending poses.

## Open questions

- How should the planner choose among multiple IK branches so the path stays continuous?
- When should a pseudoinverse or numerical optimiser replace closed-form IK at a waypoint?
- How much clearance should be added to account for link thickness and modelling uncertainty?

uke-8.title: Images and Image Processing
uke-8.summary: A digital image is a numeric array. Pixel coordinates use (u,v), with the origin at the upper-left, u increasing across columns and v increasing down rows. Histograms describe intensity distributions, thresholding produces masks, and vectorised point operations transform whole images without Python loops.
uke-8.body:
> [!abstract] TL;DR
> A digital image is a numeric array. Pixel coordinates use `(u,v)`, with the origin at the upper-left, `u` increasing across columns and `v` increasing down rows. Histograms describe intensity distributions, thresholding produces masks, and vectorised point operations transform whole images without Python loops.

## What you need to know

- A grayscale image stores one intensity per pixel; a colour image stores multiple channels, normally red, green and blue.
- Image coordinates are written `(u,v)`: `u` is the horizontal column coordinate and `v` is the vertical row coordinate. The origin is at the top-left.
- A histogram counts how many pixels occupy each intensity range and can guide the choice of a segmentation threshold.
- Monadic operations transform each pixel of one image; dyadic operations combine corresponding pixels from two images.
- The practical exercises cropping, tiling, flipping, negatives, subsampling, adding/subtracting intensity and row/column profiles using array operations.
> [!tip] Numerical implementation detail
> When subtracting unsigned integer images, convert to a signed or floating type before taking the absolute value. Otherwise negative results can wrap around. This is an implementation inference from the image data types discussed in the source.

## Key concepts

- [Digital image representation](/egb339/temaer/digital-image-representation)
- [Image histograms and thresholding](/egb339/temaer/image-histograms-and-thresholding)
- [Monadic and dyadic image operations](/egb339/temaer/monadic-and-dyadic-image-operations)
- [NumPy arrays and matrix operations](/egb339/temaer/numpy-arrays-and-matrix-operations)

## Connection to assessment

- Keep the `(u,v)` coordinate convention separate from NumPy indexing, which uses `[row, column] = [v,u]`.
- Prefer vectorised slices and Boolean masks instead of nested Python loops.
- Check image dtype and valid value range before arithmetic.
- Inspect both a histogram and the resulting mask when selecting a threshold.

## Open questions

- Which colour space will best separate coloured objects when brightness varies?
- How should noise and uneven illumination be handled before thresholding?

coppeliasim-forward-kinematics-practical.title: CoppeliaSim forward kinematics practical
coppeliasim-forward-kinematics-practical.summary: The practical code connects joint angles from three sliders to both the simulated robot and an explicitly computed end-effector position.
coppeliasim-forward-kinematics-practical.body:
The practical code connects joint angles from three sliders to both the simulated robot and an explicitly computed end-effector position.

## The model in the teach interface

With the radius in the xy-plane

`r = L1 sin(q2) + L2 cos(q3) + L3`

the position is computed as

- `x = r cos(q1)`
- `y = r sin(q1)`
- `z = L0 + L1 cos(q2) - L2 sin(q3) - L4`

The lengths are given in millimetres and divided by 1000 before display in metres. The values in the practical code must not be mixed with the measurements in Assessment 1.3.

## System connection

`CoppeliaRobot` translates `move_arm(j1, j2, j3)` into target positions for the simulator's joints via the ZMQ Remote API. [CoppeliaSim](/egb339/temaer/coppeliasim) is thus used to verify that [Forward kinematics](/egb339/temaer/forward-kinematics) is visually correct.

coppeliasim-setup.title: CoppeliaSim setup
coppeliasim-setup.summary: Install CoppeliaSim Edu 4.10.0, open prac.ttt, enable the ZMQ Remote API server and run coppeliaRobotTeach.py from the robot-practical folder. A Python process that hangs waiting for the simulator object is usually caused by ZMQ or the scene not being active.
coppeliasim-setup.body:
> [!abstract] TL;DR
> Install CoppeliaSim Edu 4.10.0, open `prac.ttt`, enable the ZMQ Remote API server and run `coppeliaRobotTeach.py` from the robot-practical folder. A Python process that hangs waiting for the simulator object is usually caused by ZMQ or the scene not being active.

## Setup sequence

1. Install CoppeliaSim **Edu 4.10.0** for the correct platform.
2. Extract the robot-practical files.
3. In CoppeliaSim, select `Modules -> Connectivity -> ZMQ remote API server`.
4. Open the scene `prac.ttt`.
5. Run `python coppeliaRobotTeach.py` from the same folder as the script.
The ZMQ server may need to be re-enabled every time CoppeliaSim is opened.

## Troubleshooting

- A message that Python is trying to fetch the `sim` object usually means the ZMQ server is not active.
- The error that an object does not exist or has an invalid alias typically occurs when `prac.ttt` is not loaded.
- When CoppeliaSim runs on Windows and Python in WSL, the client's `host` must be set to the Windows machine's IP address instead of `localhost`.
- Display scaling can be adjusted in CoppeliaSim's `usrset.txt` if the GUI does not fit.

egb339-course-and-assessment-overview.title: EGB339 course and assessment overview
egb339-course-and-assessment-overview.summary: EGB339 moves from robot kinematics in weeks 1-7 to computer vision in weeks 8-13. The assessment consists of short programming tasks (20 %), a coherent applied project (45 %) and a written exam (35 %).
egb339-course-and-assessment-overview.body:
> [!abstract] TL;DR
> EGB339 moves from robot kinematics in weeks 1-7 to computer vision in weeks 8-13. The assessment consists of short programming tasks (20 %), a coherent applied project (45 %) and a written exam (35 %).

## Assessment structure

| Assessment | Weight | Timing | Focus |
|---|---:|---|---|
| Assessment 1 - Problem-solving tasks | 20 % | Throughout the semester | 10 % robotics and 10 % computer vision |
| Assessment 2 - Applied project | 45 % | Part 1 around week 8, part 2 around week 13 | Simulated and physical robotics, then vision-guided pick-and-place |
| Assessment 3 - Written exam | 35 % | Exam period | Robotics and computer vision |

Assessment 1 builds the core algorithms that are used further in Assessment 2.
## Course progression

1. Weeks 1-3 establish linear algebra, reference frames and 2D/3D pose.
2. Weeks 4-5 cover [Forward kinematics](/egb339/temaer/forward-kinematics) and [Inverse kinematics](/egb339/temaer/inverse-kinematics).
3. Week 6 connects position and velocity through the [Robot Jacobian](/egb339/temaer/robot-jacobian).
4. Week 7 introduces [Robot motion interpolation](/egb339/temaer/robot-motion-interpolation), motion profiles and obstacle distance.
5. Weeks 8-13 build a computer vision track from images and pixel operations to features, colour, camera/image geometry and 3D vision.
## Assessment conduct

- The tasks must be solved individually and solutions must not be shared with other students.
- Any GitHub or Bitbucket repositories must be private.
- GenAI may be used for preparation, generation and improvement when the use is critically assessed, acknowledged and referenced.
- GenAI is not allowed during the individual oral components of Assessment 2.1 and 2.3.
- Assessment 2.1 and 2.3 do not have the ordinary 48-hour late submission period.
## Concepts and links

- [EGB339 Weeks 1-8 - Robotics and vision foundations](/egb339/temaer/egb339-weeks-1-8-robotics-and-vision-foundations)
- [Position, orientation and robot kinematics](/egb339/temaer/position-orientation-and-robot-kinematics)
- [Image representation and processing](/egb339/temaer/image-representation-and-processing)
- [Assessment 2 - Applied project overview](/egb339/vurderinger/assessment-2-applied-project-overview)

## Assessment 2 timeline clarification

Assessment 2.3 and 2.4 appear in the overall assessment plan because they are the later computer vision parts of the applied project. There are no separate task pages for them in the current material, so they are not treated as missing files at this point.

robot-word-typing-practical.title: Robot word typing practical
robot-word-typing-practical.summary: The scaffold separates the high-level word-typing controller from simulator and robot APIs. Each letter becomes a Cartesian key target, then a transformed robot-base target, an IK solution and a safe press motion.
robot-word-typing-practical.body:
> [!abstract] TL;DR
> The scaffold separates the high-level word-typing controller from simulator and robot APIs. Each letter becomes a Cartesian key target, then a transformed robot-base target, an IK solution and a safe press motion.

## Control flow

1. Look up the letter's position in a keyboard model.
2. Convert the point through [Keyboard coordinate mapping and safe key presses](/egb339/temaer/keyboard-coordinate-mapping-and-safe-key-presses).
3. Use [Inverse kinematics](/egb339/temaer/inverse-kinematics) to find the joint angles.
4. Move above the key, descend to press it, and lift again before lateral travel.
5. Repeat for each character and include Enter where the physical task requires it.

This is a compact motion-planning problem with explicit safe intermediate poses. The same high-level function can receive a physical Dobot object, a [CoppeliaSim](/egb339/temaer/coppeliasim) adapter or a print-based test robot, but environment-specific geometry and capabilities must remain separate.

## Assessment context

- [Assessment 2.1 - Simulation and oral demonstration](/egb339/vurderinger/assessment-2-1-simulation-and-oral-demonstration) adds the measured keyboard frame, simulation link parameters, an oral explanation and optional [Robot motion interpolation](/egb339/temaer/robot-motion-interpolation).
- [Assessment 2.2 - Physical robot submission](/egb339/vurderinger/assessment-2-2-physical-robot-submission) changes the keyboard geometry and tool offset, forbids interpolation and state getters, and imposes strict height and runtime constraints.

atan2-and-inverse-trigonometry.title: atan2 and inverse trigonometry
atan2-and-inverse-trigonometry.summary:
[!definition]
atan2(y, x) computes an angle from both Cartesian components and uses the signs to select the correct quadrant.
atan2-and-inverse-trigonometry.body:
> [!definition]
> `atan2(y, x)` computes an angle from both Cartesian components and uses the signs to select the correct quadrant.

## Why it matters

`atan(y/x)` performs the division first. Two different sign combinations can then become the same ratio, and quadrant information is lost. `atan2(y, x)` avoids this. — [Week 5 - Inverse kinematics](/egb339/uker/uke-5)

Inverse sine and cosine return only a principal value even though several angles can have the same sine or cosine. There is no `asin2` or `acos2`, so other solutions must be found using geometry, symmetry, joint limits and explicit sign choices. — [Week 5 - Inverse kinematics](/egb339/uker/uke-5)

## In the EGB339 practicals

- Use `np.atan2(y, x)` for the direction from the base to a target point.
- Clip numerical noise to `[-1, 1]` before `arccos`/`arcsin` when the theory guarantees that the argument should lie there.
- Test all quadrants and both IK branches.

## Related content

- [Inverse kinematics](/egb339/temaer/inverse-kinematics)
- [Robot workspace and IK solution branches](/egb339/temaer/robot-workspace-and-ik-solution-branches)

colour-normalization-and-chromaticity.title: Colour normalization and chromaticity
colour-normalization-and-chromaticity.summary: Colour normalization reduces the effect of overall brightness so that pixels can be compared primarily by colour proportions.
colour-normalization-and-chromaticity.body:
> [!abstract] Definition
> Colour normalization reduces the effect of overall brightness so that pixels can be compared primarily by colour proportions.

## Normalized RGB

For `s = R+G+B`, define `r=R/s`, `g=G/s` and `b=B/s` where `s>0`. Multiplying all three channels by the same brightness factor then leaves these ratios unchanged.

> [!tip] Method inference
> Assessment 1.6 requires red, green and blue squares to be counted despite brightness changes and says colour must be decoupled from intensity. Normalized chromaticity is one suitable implementation, not the only permitted solution.

Protect division where `s=0`, then classify using channel dominance or suitable ratio thresholds. - [Assessment 1.6 - Vision fundamentals part 1](/egb339/vurderinger/assessment-1-6-vision-fundamentals-part-1)

coppeliasim.title: CoppeliaSim
coppeliasim.summary: CoppeliaSim is used as a digital test arena for the Dobot Magician. The Python class CoppeliaRobot connects to the simulator through the ZMQ Remote API, fetches joint objects and sends target positions in radians.
coppeliasim.body:
CoppeliaSim is used as a digital test arena for the Dobot Magician. The Python class `CoppeliaRobot` connects to the simulator through the ZMQ Remote API, fetches joint objects and sends target positions in radians.

The simulator makes it possible to compare analytical [Forward kinematics](/egb339/temaer/forward-kinematics) with the robot's visible end-effector position before code is run on physical equipment. - [CoppeliaSim forward kinematics practical](/egb339/ressurser/coppeliasim-forward-kinematics-practical)

## Assessment 2.1

In [Assessment 2.1 - Simulation and oral demonstration](/egb339/vurderinger/assessment-2-1-simulation-and-oral-demonstration), the `prac.ttt` scene is used to validate a complete typing chain: keyboard coordinates, [frame transformation](/egb339/temaer/se-3-homogeneous-transformations), [Inverse kinematics](/egb339/temaer/inverse-kinematics) and robot motion. The keyboard's position and orientation are read from the `Plane` object. The simulation model specifies `L4=80 mm`, which is used as a downward/subtracted FK offset.

The simulator is also the arena where [joint and Cartesian interpolation](/egb339/temaer/robot-motion-interpolation) can be demonstrated before the physical transfer.

## Setup essentials

- Use CoppeliaSim Edu 4.10.0.
- Enable `Modules → Connectivity → ZMQ remote API server` and open `prac.ttt` before the Python client is started. - [CoppeliaSim setup](/egb339/ressurser/coppeliasim-setup)
- If the client hangs on connection, check the ZMQ server; if a scene object is missing, check that the correct scene is loaded. - [CoppeliaSim setup](/egb339/ressurser/coppeliasim-setup)

differential-kinematics-and-local-linear.title: Differential kinematics and local linearisation
differential-kinematics-and-local-linear.summary:
[!definition]
Differential kinematics relates small or instantaneous changes in joint coordinates to changes in end-effector coordinates using the Robot Jacobian.
differential-kinematics-and-local-linear.body:
> [!definition]
> Differential kinematics relates small or instantaneous changes in joint coordinates to changes in end-effector coordinates using the [Robot Jacobian](/egb339/temaer/robot-jacobian).

The velocity relationship is

`ṗ=J(q)q̇`.

For a short time interval, the tutorial approximates the finite changes as

- `Δp≈J(q)Δq`;
- `Δq≈J(q)⁻¹Δp` when the Jacobian is invertible;
- `pₜ₊₁≈pₜ+Δp`;
- `qₜ₊₁≈qₜ+Δq`. - [Week 6 - Robot Jacobian](/egb339/uker/uke-6)

## Why it is local

`J(q)` is evaluated at the current configuration. As the robot moves, the Jacobian changes, so a large motion cannot generally be represented accurately by one fixed linear map.

> [!tip] Practical consequence
> A Cartesian motion can be divided into sufficiently small steps, with the configuration and Jacobian updated between steps. This is an inference from the tutorial's small-timestep approximation and connects directly to [Robot motion interpolation](/egb339/temaer/robot-motion-interpolation).

## Verification

The tutorial asks for the next end-effector position to be computed in two ways: from the approximated `Δp`, and from an updated `q` followed by full [Forward kinematics](/egb339/temaer/forward-kinematics). Their difference exposes the local linearisation error. - [Week 6 - Robot Jacobian](/egb339/uker/uke-6)

dobot-magician.summary: Dobot Magician is the robot arm used in the EGB339 assignments. The course model uses three physical joint angles for base, shoulder and elbow. A mechanical parallel linkage keeps the tool axis vertical and makes Joint-angle mapping necessary.
dobot-magician.body:
Dobot Magician is the robot arm used in the EGB339 assignments. The course model uses three physical joint angles for base, shoulder and elbow. A mechanical parallel linkage keeps the tool axis vertical and makes [Joint-angle mapping](/egb339/temaer/joint-angle-mapping) necessary.

The robot's end effector can, among other things, be a pen/stylus or a suction cup. It is controlled through `move_arm(j1, j2, j3)` in the provided API and can be tested in [CoppeliaSim](/egb339/temaer/coppeliasim).

| Environment | `L0` | `L1` | `L2` | `L3` | `L4` |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| CoppeliaSim suction gripper | 138 | 135 | 147 | 60 | -80 |
| Physical stylus holder | 138 | 135 | 147 | 60 | -70 |

All measurements in the table are in millimetres. The differing `L4` value means that the simulation model cannot be transferred to the physical robot without an explicit configuration switch. - [Assessment 2.1 - Simulation and oral demonstration](/egb339/vurderinger/assessment-2-1-simulation-and-oral-demonstration) and [Assessment 2.2 - Physical robot submission](/egb339/vurderinger/assessment-2-2-physical-robot-submission)

egb339-weeks-1-5-robotics-foundations.summary: Linear algebra → SO(2)/SE(2) → SO(3)/SE(3) → pose graphs → forward kinematics → inverse kinematics
egb339-weeks-1-5-robotics-foundations.body:
> [!abstract] Learning path
> `Linear algebra → SO(2)/SE(2) → SO(3)/SE(3) → pose graphs → forward kinematics → inverse kinematics`

## Week-by-week map

1. [Week 1 - Unit introduction and kinematics context](/egb339/uker/uke-1) establishes the robotics and assessment context.
2. [Week 2 - Linear algebra and 2D pose](/egb339/uker/uke-2) introduces [Linear algebra for robotics](/egb339/temaer/linear-algebra-for-robotics), [SO(2) rotation matrices](/egb339/temaer/so-2-rotation-matrices) and [SE(2) homogeneous transformations](/egb339/temaer/se-2-homogeneous-transformations).
3. [Week 3 - NumPy and 3D pose](/egb339/uker/uke-3) extends to [SO(3) rotation matrices](/egb339/temaer/so-3-rotation-matrices), [SE(3) homogeneous transformations](/egb339/temaer/se-3-homogeneous-transformations), [Rotation composition in 3D](/egb339/temaer/rotation-composition-in-3d) and [Pose graphs](/egb339/temaer/pose-graphs).
4. [Week 4 - Forward kinematics](/egb339/uker/uke-4) uses [Kinematic chains and joints](/egb339/temaer/kinematic-chains-and-joints) to calculate the end-effector pose.
5. [Week 5 - Inverse kinematics](/egb339/uker/uke-5) goes from a desired target back to joint values and introduces [atan2 and inverse trigonometry](/egb339/temaer/atan2-and-inverse-trigonometry) as well as [Robot workspace and IK solution branches](/egb339/temaer/robot-workspace-and-ik-solution-branches).

## The central dependency

[Reference frames](/egb339/temaer/reference-frames) determines what the coordinates mean. Rotation and transformation matrices move information between the frames. Pose graphs organise the transformations. Forward kinematics follows the chain from joints to end effector; inverse kinematics solves the same geometry in the opposite direction.

## Practical system

[Dobot Magician](/egb339/temaer/dobot-magician) is the physical robot model, and [CoppeliaSim](/egb339/temaer/coppeliasim) provides visual control of the kinematics. See also [CoppeliaSim forward kinematics practical](/egb339/ressurser/coppeliasim-forward-kinematics-practical), [Assessment 1.3 - Dobot forward kinematics](/egb339/vurderinger/assessment-1-3-dobot-forward-kinematics) and [Robot word typing practical](/egb339/ressurser/robot-word-typing-practical).

## Common failure modes

- wrong frame direction or a forgotten inverse;
- wrong order for 3D rotations;
- `*` used instead of `@` in NumPy;
- hard-coded example data instead of general function logic;
- mixed units or angle conventions;
- only one IK branch or the wrong quadrant from inverse trigonometry.

forward-kinematics.title: Forward kinematics
forward-kinematics.summary:
[!definition]
Forward kinematics computes the end effector's pose or position from known joint values and robot geometry.
forward-kinematics.body:
> [!definition]
> Forward kinematics computes the end effector's pose or position from known joint values and robot geometry.

## How it works

For a serial robot, the transformation from base to tool is built as `T₀E = T₀1 T₁2 … TₙE`. Each factor describes one rotation, translation or combined joint/link transformation. The order follows the physical chain from base to end effector. — [Week 4 - Forward kinematics](/egb339/uker/uke-4)

The final position is the translation column of `T₀E`, while the rotation block describes the end effector's orientation.

## In the EGB339 practicals

EGB339 uses both an explicit trigonometric Dobot model and a general `SE(3)` chain. They express the same geometry, but can have different dimensions, zero angles and model variables. — [CoppeliaSim forward kinematics practical](/egb339/ressurser/coppeliasim-forward-kinematics-practical)

FK is also the most important verification of [Inverse kinematics](/egb339/temaer/inverse-kinematics): joint values from IK should give the target pose when inserted into FK.

## Differential view

When FK is written as `p=FK(q)`, the [Robot Jacobian](/egb339/temaer/robot-jacobian) is the derivative `∂p/∂q`. FK thus describes the position map itself, while the Jacobian describes how small or instantaneous joint changes affect the end effector. - [Week 6 - Robot Jacobian](/egb339/uker/uke-6)

image-histograms-and-thresholding.title: Image histograms and thresholding
image-histograms-and-thresholding.summary: An image histogram counts pixel intensities. Thresholding compares pixels with a selected value to produce a Boolean or binary segmentation mask.
image-histograms-and-thresholding.body:
> [!abstract] Definition
> An image histogram counts pixel intensities. Thresholding compares pixels with a selected value to produce a Boolean or binary segmentation mask.

## Workflow

1. Inspect the image and its intensity histogram.
2. Choose a threshold between the distributions belonging to foreground and background.
3. Form a mask such as `mask = image < threshold` or `image > threshold`.
4. Inspect the mask and adjust for noise or illumination variation. - [Week 8 - Images and image processing](/egb339/uker/uke-8)

## Limitations

- One global threshold can fail under uneven lighting.
- Histogram peaks may overlap when object and background intensities are similar.
- Colour segmentation may require more than one channel or a representation less sensitive to intensity.

inverse-kinematics.title: Inverse kinematics
inverse-kinematics.summary:
[!definition]
Inverse kinematics finds joint values that place the end effector at a desired position or pose. This is the inverse direction of Forward kinematics.
inverse-kinematics.body:
> [!definition]
> Inverse kinematics finds joint values that place the end effector at a desired position or pose. This is the inverse direction of [Forward kinematics](/egb339/temaer/forward-kinematics).

## Methods

- Numerical approximation iterates from an initial guess and mainly requires that FK is known.
- Algebraic rearrangement attempts to isolate the joint variables directly.
- Geometric analysis divides the robot into triangles and uses trigonometric relations. — [Week 5 - Inverse kinematics](/egb339/uker/uke-5)

[Assessment 1.4 - Robot inverse kinematics](/egb339/vurderinger/assessment-1-4-robot-inverse-kinematics) implements both numerical cost minimisation and geometric IK, making [Optimization-based inverse kinematics](/egb339/temaer/optimization-based-inverse-kinematics) the explicit bridge between FK error and a usable joint solution.

## Solutions and reachability

A target can have no solution, one degenerate solution, or several solutions such as elbow up/elbow down. This connects IK directly to [Robot workspace and IK solution branches](/egb339/temaer/robot-workspace-and-ik-solution-branches) and [atan2 and inverse trigonometry](/egb339/temaer/atan2-and-inverse-trigonometry). — [Week 5 - Inverse kinematics](/egb339/uker/uke-5)

## In the EGB339 practicals

In the typing task, IK is used between the key's Cartesian coordinate and `move_arm(j1, j2, j3)`. The motion is planned as above the key → touch → above the key. - [Robot word typing practical](/egb339/ressurser/robot-word-typing-practical)

[Assessment 2.1 - Simulation and oral demonstration](/egb339/vurderinger/assessment-2-1-simulation-and-oral-demonstration) requires that the key points first be transformed from the keyboard's reference frame to the robot base. IK then solves the joint angles for each transformed target. The physical transfer in [Assessment 2.2 - Physical robot submission](/egb339/vurderinger/assessment-2-2-physical-robot-submission) uses the same overall chain, but with different tool parameters, stricter safety limits and fewer available API methods.

## Robustness and constraints

Targets outside the workspace must be detected and handled instead of being passed on as invalid joint commands. The oral part of Assessment 2.1 also expects the student to be able to explain how optimisation-based IK can be extended with joint limits or obstacle avoidance. - [Assessment 2.1 - Simulation and oral demonstration](/egb339/vurderinger/assessment-2-1-simulation-and-oral-demonstration)

keyboard-coordinate-mapping-and-safe-key.title: Keyboard coordinate mapping and safe key presses
keyboard-coordinate-mapping-and-safe-key.summary:
[!definition]
Keyboard coordinate mapping converts a key label into a point in the keyboard frame, transforms it into the robot base frame, and passes the resulting target to Inverse kinematics.
keyboard-coordinate-mapping-and-safe-key.body:
> [!definition]
> Keyboard coordinate mapping converts a key label into a point in the keyboard frame, transforms it into the robot base frame, and passes the resulting target to [Inverse kinematics](/egb339/temaer/inverse-kinematics).

## Coordinate pipeline

`letter → key centre in pixels → key point in millimetres → homogeneous frame transform → robot-base point → IK → joint command`

In the simulation, the keyboard image is measured relative to a chosen origin and scaled using the `120×290 mm` keyboard size. The keyboard object's pose in [CoppeliaSim](/egb339/temaer/coppeliasim) then supplies the frame relationship. - [Assessment 2.1 - Simulation and oral demonstration](/egb339/vurderinger/assessment-2-1-simulation-and-oral-demonstration)

For the physical system, the keyboard-frame origin is `(248,-77.25) mm` in the robot frame and the keyboard is rotated 90° about z. - [Assessment 2.2 - Physical robot submission](/egb339/vurderinger/assessment-2-2-physical-robot-submission)

## Simulation versus physical configuration

| Concern | Simulation 2.1 | Physical 2.2 |
|---|---|---|
| Keyboard geometry | Measure image and scale from `120×290 mm` | Letter keys `16.2×11.5 mm`; Enter width `19.0 mm` |
| Tool offset | `L4=80 mm`, applied downward in FK | Source convention `L4=-70 mm` |
| Motion extension | Joint and Cartesian interpolation for top band | Interpolation explicitly forbidden |
| State getters | Available through simulator API | `get_joint_config()` and `get_end_effector_pose()` unavailable |
| Timing | Simulator-dependent | `move_arm` is blocking; no `sleep()` |

The shared lengths are `L0=138`, `L1=135`, `L2=147` and `L3=60 mm`. The `L4` signs must not be compared without also checking how each FK equation applies the offset. - [Assessment 2.1 - Simulation and oral demonstration](/egb339/vurderinger/assessment-2-1-simulation-and-oral-demonstration) and [Assessment 2.2 - Physical robot submission](/egb339/vurderinger/assessment-2-2-physical-robot-submission)

## Safe press pattern

1. Move above the target key.
2. Descend vertically to the press height.
3. Lift vertically before any lateral travel.
4. Move sideways only after the required clearance has been reached.

For the physical robot, the press plane is `z=0`, commands below `z=-5 mm` abort the run, and sideways motion requires the stylus to be at least `z=10 mm`. - [Assessment 2.2 - Physical robot submission](/egb339/vurderinger/assessment-2-2-physical-robot-submission)

## Robust implementation boundary

> [!tip] Configuration separation
> Keep key geometry, frame transform, link parameters and API capabilities in an environment-specific configuration. The high-level sequence can then remain shared while the simulation and physical constraints stay explicit. This is a synthesis of [Assessment 2.1 - Simulation and oral demonstration](/egb339/vurderinger/assessment-2-1-simulation-and-oral-demonstration) and [Assessment 2.2 - Physical robot submission](/egb339/vurderinger/assessment-2-2-physical-robot-submission).

kinematic-chains-and-joints.title: Kinematic chains and joints
kinematic-chains-and-joints.summary:
[!definition]
A kinematic chain models a robot as rigid links connected by joints. Each joint contributes a variable transformation, while the link geometry usually provides fixed transformations.
kinematic-chains-and-joints.body:
> [!definition]
> A kinematic chain models a robot as rigid links connected by joints. Each joint contributes a variable transformation, while the link geometry usually provides fixed transformations.

## How it works

- A revolute joint contributes a rotation `R(q)`.
- A prismatic joint contributes a translation that depends on `q`.
- A fixed link contributes a known length and possibly a fixed angular offset.
- Serial transformations are multiplied from the base towards the end effector. — [Week 4 - Forward kinematics](/egb339/uker/uke-4)

The frame choice is not unique, but all choices must be consistent. Passive mechanical linkages can give dependent model angles and a need for [Joint-angle mapping](/egb339/temaer/joint-angle-mapping).

linear-algebra-for-robotics.title: Linear algebra for robotics
linear-algebra-for-robotics.summary:
[!definition]
Linear algebra provides the language for representing points, directions, orientations and transformations with vectors and matrices.
linear-algebra-for-robotics.body:
> [!definition]
> Linear algebra provides the language for representing points, directions, orientations and transformations with vectors and matrices.

## Why it matters

Robotics requires that quantities expressed in one coordinate frame can be converted to another. Matrix multiplication composes these operations and makes long transformation chains systematic. — [Week 2 - Linear algebra and 2D pose](/egb339/uker/uke-2)

## How it works

- A dot product gives one number from two equally long vectors.
- A matrix product is computed as dot products between rows and columns.
- For `A` with shape `m×n` and `B` with shape `n×p`, `AB` has shape `m×p`.
- Transposition swaps rows and columns.
- The inverse undoes a transformation when it exists.
- The determinant says, among other things, whether a square matrix is invertible and whether an orthogonal transformation preserves or mirrors orientation.

## In the EGB339 practicals

The Python functions are expected to use general matrices and vectors. Numerical matrix properties should be checked with tolerance. — [Week 2 - Linear algebra and 2D pose](/egb339/uker/uke-2)

The warmup's Q11-Q15 introduce the NumPy operations that implement this mathematics: transposition, determinant, inverse, broadcasting and ordinary matrix multiplication. - [Assessment 1.0 - Warmup to Gradescope](/egb339/vurderinger/assessment-1-0-warmup-to-gradescope)

monadic-and-dyadic-image-operations.summary: A monadic operation maps one input image to an output pixel by pixel. A dyadic operation combines corresponding pixels from two input images.
monadic-and-dyadic-image-operations.body:
> [!abstract] Definition
> A monadic operation maps one input image to an output pixel by pixel. A dyadic operation combines corresponding pixels from two input images.

## Examples

- Monadic: negative, brightness shift, threshold, clipping or type conversion. - [Week 8 - Images and image processing](/egb339/uker/uke-8)
- Dyadic: addition, subtraction, absolute difference or masking with a second array. - [Week 8 - Images and image processing](/egb339/uker/uke-8)
- Vectorised NumPy expressions apply these operations to complete arrays without explicit pixel loops. - [Week 8 - Images and image processing](/egb339/uker/uke-8)

> [!warning] Unsigned subtraction
> Convert unsigned images to a signed or floating dtype before subtraction; otherwise values below zero can wrap around.

numpy-arrays-and-matrix-operations.title: NumPy arrays and matrix operations
numpy-arrays-and-matrix-operations.summary:
[!definition]
A NumPy array stores numerical data with an explicit shape and data type (dtype). In EGB339, arrays are used for vectors, rotation matrices and homogeneous transformations.
numpy-arrays-and-matrix-operations.body:
> [!definition]
> A NumPy array stores numerical data with an explicit shape (`shape`) and data type (`dtype`). In EGB339, arrays are used for vectors, rotation matrices and homogeneous transformations.

## How it works

- `np.array([...])` creates an array.
- `.shape` distinguishes for example `(3,)`, `(3, 1)` and `(3, 3)`.
- `A @ B` is matrix multiplication.
- `A * B` is element-wise multiplication.
- `reshape`, slicing and indexing change or select how data is interpreted.
- `np.allclose` and `np.isclose` compare floating-point numbers with tolerance.

Broadcasting can expand dimensions automatically. It is useful, but can also hide a shape error because the expression still runs. — [Week 3 - NumPy and 3D pose](/egb339/uker/uke-3)

## In the EGB339 practicals

Check the shapes at the function boundaries. Use `@` for rotation of points and composition of transformations; `np.array` is the constructor, not the operation itself.

Q8-Q15 in [Assessment 1.0 - Warmup to Gradescope](/egb339/vurderinger/assessment-1-0-warmup-to-gradescope) train array creation, `np.float64`, desired `shape`, element-wise arithmetic, transposition, determinant, inverse, broadcasting and matrix multiplication. Q15 asks for the product `AB`, so the relevant operator is `A @ B`, not `A * B`.

In Week 8, the same array mechanisms represent images. Slicing performs cropping and subsampling, Boolean masks perform thresholding, and the channel axis separates the colour components. `dtype` must be checked before image arithmetic because unsigned integer operations can wrap. - [Week 8 - Images and image processing](/egb339/uker/uke-8)

optimization-based-inverse-kinematics.title: Optimization-based inverse kinematics
optimization-based-inverse-kinematics.summary: Numerical inverse kinematics searches for joint angles that minimise the difference between a target pose and the pose produced by Forward kinematics.
optimization-based-inverse-kinematics.body:
> [!abstract] Definition
> Numerical inverse kinematics searches for joint angles that minimise the difference between a target pose and the pose produced by [Forward kinematics](/egb339/temaer/forward-kinematics).

## Core model

For a position-only target `p*`, a simple cost is

`c(θ) = ||FK(θ) - p*||₂`.

An optimiser such as `scipy.optimize.fmin` changes `θ` until this cost is small. The assessment contrasts this method with geometric IK. - [Assessment 1.4 - Robot inverse kinematics](/egb339/vurderinger/assessment-1-4-robot-inverse-kinematics)

## Practical implications

- The starting guess matters because a nonlinear problem may contain several IK branches or local minima. - [Assessment 1.4 - Robot inverse kinematics](/egb339/vurderinger/assessment-1-4-robot-inverse-kinematics)
- Joint-limit penalties, obstacle penalties or orientation error can be added to the cost when the basic position error is insufficient.
- Always verify the returned angles by running FK and measuring the final error. - [Assessment 1.4 - Robot inverse kinematics](/egb339/vurderinger/assessment-1-4-robot-inverse-kinematics)

> [!tip] Synthesis
> Adding penalties is a general extension of the assessment's optimisation formulation, not a requirement explicitly imposed by Assessment 1.4.

partial-derivatives-for-robotics.title: Partial derivatives for robotics
partial-derivatives-for-robotics.summary:
[!definition]
A partial derivative differentiates a multivariable function with respect to one variable while treating the remaining variables as constants.
partial-derivatives-for-robotics.body:
> [!definition]
> A partial derivative differentiates a multivariable function with respect to one variable while treating the remaining variables as constants.

For `f(x,y)=3x²+2y³`, the source gives

- `∂f/∂x = 6x`;
- `∂f/∂y = 6y²`. - [Week 6 - Robot Jacobian](/egb339/uker/uke-6)

A robot's forward-kinematics position contains several joint variables in each output coordinate. Taking every output derivative with respect to every joint variable forms the [Robot Jacobian](/egb339/temaer/robot-jacobian).

For a vector function `p(q)` with `m` output coordinates and `n` joint variables,

`Jᵢⱼ = ∂pᵢ/∂qⱼ`,

so the resulting Jacobian has shape `m×n`. - [Week 6 - Robot Jacobian](/egb339/uker/uke-6)

## Relevant derivative rules

The constant, power, product, quotient, chain and linear-separability rules remain valid. For trigonometric robot models, the especially frequent identities are `d(sin x)/dx=cos x` and `d(cos x)/dx=-sin x`. - [Week 6 - Robot Jacobian](/egb339/uker/uke-6)

## Symbolic workflow

SymPy can construct the matrix from symbolic FK expressions with `.jacobian()` and then evaluate it for a configuration with `.subs()`. The symbolic result should be compared with the hand-derived matrix. - [Week 6 - Robot Jacobian](/egb339/uker/uke-6)

planar-homographies.title: Planar homographies
planar-homographies.summary: A planar homography is a nonsingular 3×3 matrix that maps points between two planes in homogeneous coordinates, up to an arbitrary nonzero scale.
planar-homographies.body:
> [!abstract] Definition
> A planar homography is a nonsingular `3×3` matrix that maps points between two planes in homogeneous coordinates, up to an arbitrary nonzero scale.

## Course convention

Assessment 1.7 uses `p ~ Hq`, where `q` is a point on the work surface and `p` is its image coordinate. - [Assessment 1.7 - Vision fundamentals part 2](/egb339/vurderinger/assessment-1-7-vision-fundamentals-part-2)

- Surface to image: form homogeneous `q`, compute `p̃ = Hq`, then divide by `p̃₃`.
- Image to surface: form homogeneous `p`, compute `q̃ = H⁻¹p`, then divide by `q̃₃`.
- The normalization step is essential because homogeneous vectors represent the same point under nonzero scaling.

The assessment uses the inverse mapping to recover triangle vertices on the work surface and calculate their physical area. - [Assessment 1.7 - Vision fundamentals part 2](/egb339/vurderinger/assessment-1-7-vision-fundamentals-part-2)

point-to-segment-distance-and-obstacle-c.title: Point-to-segment distance and obstacle clearance
point-to-segment-distance-and-obstacle-c.summary: Approximate a robot link as the segment from P₁ to P₂ and an obstacle as point O; the minimum distance provides a simple collision-clearance measure.
point-to-segment-distance-and-obstacle-c.body:
> [!abstract] Definition
> Approximate a robot link as the segment from `P₁` to `P₂` and an obstacle as point `O`; the minimum distance provides a simple collision-clearance measure.

## Projection method

Let `B = P₂-P₁` and `A = O-P₁`. The projection parameter is

`t = (A·B)/(B·B)`.

Clamp `t` to `[0,1]`, form the closest point `C = P₁+tB`, and calculate `d = ||O-C||₂`.

> [!tip] Mathematical completion
> Week 7 introduces projection and link-to-obstacle distance. Clamping is required when the closest point on the infinite line lies beyond either end of the physical link segment.

## Planning use

- Evaluate every link at every sampled configuration. - [Week 7 - Motion planning](/egb339/uker/uke-7)
- Treat `d` below a chosen safety margin as a collision risk.
- A point obstacle and zero-thickness link are simplified models; real geometry needs additional margin.

pose-graphs.title: Pose graphs
pose-graphs.summary:
[!definition]
A pose graph represents coordinate frames as nodes and known transformations as directed connections. An unknown pose is found by following a valid path and multiplying the transformations in the correct order.
pose-graphs.body:
> [!definition]
> A pose graph represents coordinate frames as nodes and known transformations as directed connections. An unknown pose is found by following a valid path and multiplying the transformations in the correct order.

## How it works

If `{B}` is known relative to `{A}` and `{C}` relative to `{B}`, the transformation from `{C}` to `{A}` can be built as an ordered product. The neighbouring symbols in the frame annotation must cancel/match. When moving against an available edge, the inverse is used. — [Week 3 - NumPy and 3D pose](/egb339/uker/uke-3)

## Why it matters

Pose graphs scale from a point observed by a robot sensor to entire [Kinematic chains and joints](/egb339/temaer/kinematic-chains-and-joints). [Forward kinematics](/egb339/temaer/forward-kinematics) is a pose graph in which certain edges depend on joint variables. — [Week 4 - Forward kinematics](/egb339/uker/uke-4)

position-orientation-and-robot-kinematic.body:
## Representation

- [Reference frames](/egb339/temaer/reference-frames) describes where coordinates apply.
- [SO(2) rotation matrices](/egb339/temaer/so-2-rotation-matrices) and [SE(2) homogeneous transformations](/egb339/temaer/se-2-homogeneous-transformations) establish the 2D model.
- [SO(3) rotation matrices](/egb339/temaer/so-3-rotation-matrices) describes orientation.
- [SE(3) homogeneous transformations](/egb339/temaer/se-3-homogeneous-transformations) describes pose: orientation and position together.
- [Pose graphs](/egb339/temaer/pose-graphs) organises composed transformations.

## Robot chain

- [Joint-angle mapping](/egb339/temaer/joint-angle-mapping) translates the physical robot into model variables.
- [Forward kinematics](/egb339/temaer/forward-kinematics) maps joint values to end-effector pose.
- [Inverse kinematics](/egb339/temaer/inverse-kinematics) maps a desired end-effector pose to joint values.

## Differential motion

- [Partial derivatives for robotics](/egb339/temaer/partial-derivatives-for-robotics) builds the calculus foundation.
- [Robot Jacobian](/egb339/temaer/robot-jacobian) maps joint velocity to Cartesian velocity.
- [Differential kinematics and local linearisation](/egb339/temaer/differential-kinematics-and-local-linearisation) approximates small motion steps.
- [Robot motion interpolation](/egb339/temaer/robot-motion-interpolation) compares paths built in joint and Cartesian coordinates.
- [Trapezoidal motion profiles](/egb339/temaer/trapezoidal-motion-profiles) supplies time parametrisation, while [Point-to-segment distance and obstacle clearance](/egb339/temaer/point-to-segment-distance-and-obstacle-clearance) introduces a simple geometric collision check. - [Week 7 - Motion planning](/egb339/uker/uke-7)

## Applied project

[Keyboard coordinate mapping and safe key presses](/egb339/temaer/keyboard-coordinate-mapping-and-safe-key-presses) applies reference frames, homogeneous transformations and IK to [Assessment 2.1 - Simulation and oral demonstration](/egb339/vurderinger/assessment-2-1-simulation-and-oral-demonstration) and [Assessment 2.2 - Physical robot submission](/egb339/vurderinger/assessment-2-2-physical-robot-submission). The shared controller is summarised in [Robot word typing practical](/egb339/ressurser/robot-word-typing-practical), while environment-specific geometry and safety rules remain explicit.

public-and-private-autograder-tests.title: Public and private autograder tests
public-and-private-autograder-tests.summary: Public tests are visible local checks that catch basic errors. Private tests are hidden cases that Gradescope uses to verify that the implementation follows the general contract, not just the examples.
public-and-private-autograder-tests.body:
> [!abstract] Definition
> Public tests are visible local checks that catch basic errors. Private tests are hidden cases that Gradescope uses to verify that the implementation follows the general contract, not just the examples.

## Workflow

1. Keep the correct file name, function name and signature.
2. Implement the function from the docstring and the task text.
3. Run the public tests and fix import, return, type and simple value errors.
4. Add your own tests for boundaries, shapes and alternative inputs.
5. Submit on Gradescope for the private tests. - [Assessment 1.0 - Warmup to Gradescope](/egb339/vurderinger/assessment-1-0-warmup-to-gradescope)

## What passing public tests means

Public tests are a necessary local check, but they do not guarantee that the hidden tests pass. A solution that hardcodes the examples can pass a simple visible test and still fail on new inputs. - [Assessment 1.0 - Warmup to Gradescope](/egb339/vurderinger/assessment-1-0-warmup-to-gradescope)

> [!tip] Submission strategy
> Use your own test cases before uploading. [Assessment 1 - Problem-solving task overview](/egb339/vurderinger/assessment-1-problem-solving-task-overview) gives five combined Gradescope attempts without penalty for each coding task, so local tests reduce unnecessary attempts.

python-control-flow-and-collections.title: Python control flow and collections
python-control-flow-and-collections.summary: Control flow determines which code blocks run and how many times they run. Lists and tuples collect multiple values that functions can produce or process.
python-control-flow-and-collections.body:
> [!abstract] Definition
> Control flow determines which code blocks run and how many times they run. Lists and tuples collect multiple values that functions can produce or process.

## Core mechanisms

- An `if` statement selects code based on a Boolean expression.
- `and` combines requirements that must both be true; `or` requires at least one to be true.
- A `while` loop continues as long as the condition is true.
- A `for` loop iterates through the elements of a collection.
- A list is mutable and can be extended with `.append()`; a tuple is a fixed sequence.
- A function collects reusable logic and returns the result with `return`. - [Assessment 1.0 - Warmup to Gradescope](/egb339/vurderinger/assessment-1-0-warmup-to-gradescope)

## Assessment use

Q2-Q7 in [Assessment 1.0 - Warmup to Gradescope](/egb339/vurderinger/assessment-1-0-warmup-to-gradescope) test these mechanisms with new input values. Conditions and loops should therefore use the function argument, not copy the example results.

reference-frames.title: Reference frames
reference-frames.summary: A physical point is the same regardless of coordinate system, but the coordinate vector depends on the frame.
reference-frames.body:
A physical point is the same regardless of coordinate system, but the coordinate vector depends on the frame.

If `R` describes the orientation of frame `{A}` relative to `{0}`, then

- `p₀ = R p_A` when the origins coincide;
- `p_A = Rᵀ p₀` in the opposite direction;
- `p₀ = R p_A + t` when the frames are also translated.

The most important thing is to state clearly which frame each vector is expressed in. This makes the multiplication order and the need for the inverse easier to check. — [Week 2 - Linear algebra and 2D pose](/egb339/uker/uke-2)

See [SO(3) rotation matrices](/egb339/temaer/so-3-rotation-matrices) and [SE(3) homogeneous transformations](/egb339/temaer/se-3-homogeneous-transformations).

In [Assessment 1.1 - Position and orientation in 2D](/egb339/vurderinger/assessment-1-1-position-and-orientation-in-2d) the point is given in one frame and requested in another. The illustration figures do not provide test data; they show why the frame direction must be determined in general.

robot-jacobian.title: Robot Jacobian
robot-jacobian.summary:
[!definition]
The robot Jacobian is the matrix derivative of Forward kinematics. It maps instantaneous joint velocity q̇ to end-effector velocity ṗ through ṗ=J(q)q̇.
robot-jacobian.body:
> [!definition]
> The robot Jacobian is the matrix derivative of [Forward kinematics](/egb339/temaer/forward-kinematics). It maps instantaneous joint velocity `q̇` to end-effector velocity `ṗ` through `ṗ=J(q)q̇`.

## Construction

If `p=FK(q)` is a vector, every Jacobian entry is a [partial derivative](/egb339/temaer/partial-derivatives-for-robotics):

`Jᵢⱼ(q)=∂pᵢ/∂qⱼ`.

The matrix depends on the current joint configuration because the derivatives normally contain the joint variables themselves. - [Week 6 - Robot Jacobian](/egb339/uker/uke-6)

For the source's planar two-link arm,

`pₓ=L₁cos(θ₁)+L₂cos(θ₁+θ₂)`

`pᵧ=L₁sin(θ₁)+L₂sin(θ₁+θ₂)`.

> [!tip] Derived from the source model
> Applying the stated derivative rules gives
> `J = [[-L₁sin(θ₁)-L₂sin(θ₁+θ₂), -L₂sin(θ₁+θ₂)], [L₁cos(θ₁)+L₂cos(θ₁+θ₂), L₂cos(θ₁+θ₂)]]`.
> This explicit matrix is derived from the FK equations in [Week 6 - Robot Jacobian](/egb339/uker/uke-6).

## Forward and inverse velocity mapping

- `ṗ=J(q)q̇` computes Cartesian velocity from joint velocity.
- `q̇=J(q)⁻¹ṗ` computes joint velocity from Cartesian velocity only when the Jacobian is square and non-singular under the source's ordinary-inverse treatment. - [Week 6 - Robot Jacobian](/egb339/uker/uke-6)

Rotational joint velocities must be in radians per second for mathematical consistency. - [Week 6 - Robot Jacobian](/egb339/uker/uke-6)

## Singularity

At a singular configuration, `J(q)` has no ordinary inverse. The forward velocity mapping still exists, but the inverse mapping used in the tutorial cannot be applied directly. - [Week 6 - Robot Jacobian](/egb339/uker/uke-6)

robot-motion-interpolation.title: Robot motion interpolation
robot-motion-interpolation.summary:
[!definition]
Motion interpolation generates intermediate motion targets between a start and goal, either in joint space or in Cartesian task space.
robot-motion-interpolation.body:
> [!definition]
> Motion interpolation generates intermediate motion targets between a start and goal, either in joint space or in Cartesian task space.

## Joint interpolation

Joint interpolation constructs intermediate `q` values and sends them through the robot model. The corresponding end-effector path is determined by [Forward kinematics](/egb339/temaer/forward-kinematics).

> [!tip] Path implication
> A path that is simple in joint coordinates is not generally a straight line in Cartesian space because FK is non-linear. This is shown directly in [Week 7 - Motion planning](/egb339/uker/uke-7).

## Cartesian interpolation

Cartesian interpolation constructs intermediate end-effector targets `p`. Each target then requires a corresponding joint configuration from [Inverse kinematics](/egb339/temaer/inverse-kinematics) or a local joint update from [Differential kinematics and local linearisation](/egb339/temaer/differential-kinematics-and-local-linearisation).

For `n` samples, a straight Cartesian path can use `pᵢ = pₛ + (pₑ-pₛ)i/(n-1)` for `i=0,…,n-1`. - [Week 7 - Motion planning](/egb339/uker/uke-7)

## Assessment boundary

[Assessment 2.1 - Simulation and oral demonstration](/egb339/vurderinger/assessment-2-1-simulation-and-oral-demonstration) asks students targeting the highest functional band to demonstrate both joint- and Cartesian-interpolated motion between letters. [Assessment 2.2 - Physical robot submission](/egb339/vurderinger/assessment-2-2-physical-robot-submission) explicitly forbids using either interpolation mode on the physical task.

> [!warning]
> Treat interpolation as a simulation demonstration feature for Assessment 2.1, not as code to carry unchanged into the physical submission.

robot-workspace-and-ik-solution-branches.title: Robot workspace and IK solution branches
robot-workspace-and-ik-solution-branches.summary:
[!definition]
The workspace is the set of positions or poses a robot can physically reach. An IK branch is one connected family of joint configurations that produce the target pose, for example elbow up or elbow down.
robot-workspace-and-ik-solution-branches.body:
> [!definition]
> The workspace is the set of positions or poses a robot can physically reach. An IK branch is one connected family of joint configurations that produce the target pose, for example elbow up or elbow down.

## How it works

For a planar two-link robot with lengths `L1` and `L2` and target distance `r`, geometric reach normally requires `|L1 - L2| ≤ r ≤ L1 + L2`. Within this range, the same point can often have two mirrored solutions. At the boundaries the branches can coincide; outside it, no real geometric solution exists. — [Week 5 - Inverse kinematics](/egb339/uker/uke-5)

The physical workspace can be smaller than the geometric one because of joint limits, collisions and mechanical couplings.

## In the EGB339 practicals

An IK function should distinguish between "no solution" and a valid solution, handle both required branches and verify each solution with [Forward kinematics](/egb339/temaer/forward-kinematics).

## Related content

- [Inverse kinematics](/egb339/temaer/inverse-kinematics)
- [atan2 and inverse trigonometry](/egb339/temaer/atan2-and-inverse-trigonometry)
- [Dobot Magician](/egb339/temaer/dobot-magician)

rotation-composition-in-3d.title: Rotation composition in 3D
rotation-composition-in-3d.summary:
[!definition]
Composed 3D rotations are ordered products of rotation matrices. The product depends both on the rotation order and on whether each axis is interpreted in the new/local or old/global frame.
rotation-composition-in-3d.body:
> [!definition]
> Composed 3D rotations are ordered products of rotation matrices. The product depends both on the rotation order and on whether each axis is interpreted in the new/local or old/global frame.

## Why it matters

Rotations about different axes normally do not commute: `R_x(α) @ R_z(β)` is not the same as `R_z(β) @ R_x(α)`. — [Week 3 - NumPy and 3D pose](/egb339/uker/uke-3)

## How it works

- A rotation about a new/local axis is placed on the side that follows the course notation's chain.
- A rotation about an old/global axis is placed on the opposite side.
- The safe method is to draw the frames, name the transformations and check that the frame indices match before multiplying.

> [!warning]
> Do not use a memorised "always left" or "always right" rule without checking EGB339's notation and the wording of the task.

## Related content

- [SO(3) rotation matrices](/egb339/temaer/so-3-rotation-matrices)
- [Reference frames](/egb339/temaer/reference-frames)
- [Pose graphs](/egb339/temaer/pose-graphs)

se-2-homogeneous-transformations.title: SE(2) homogeneous transformations
se-2-homogeneous-transformations.summary:
[!definition]
SE(2) describes a full 2D pose by combining rotation and translation into a single homogeneous 3×3 matrix.
se-2-homogeneous-transformations.body:
> [!definition]
> `SE(2)` describes a full 2D pose by combining rotation and translation into a single homogeneous `3×3` matrix.

## How it works

`T = [[R, t], [0, 0, 1]]`, where `R ∈ SO(2)` and `t ∈ ℝ²`.

A point `p = [x, y]ᵀ` is extended to `p_h = [x, y, 1]ᵀ`. Then `T @ p_h` performs both rotation and translation. The last coordinate is `1` for points and `0` for pure direction vectors. — [Week 2 - Linear algebra and 2D pose](/egb339/uker/uke-2)

## Why it matters

Homogeneous matrices turn pose composition into ordinary matrix multiplication and are the direct 2D predecessor of [SE(3) homogeneous transformations](/egb339/temaer/se-3-homogeneous-transformations).

[Assessment 1.1 - Position and orientation in 2D](/egb339/vurderinger/assessment-1-1-position-and-orientation-in-2d) uses `SE(2)` both to construct a 2D rigid-body transformation and to express a point in a rotated and translated frame. The direction determines whether `T` or `T⁻¹` should be used.

## Related content

- [SO(2) rotation matrices](/egb339/temaer/so-2-rotation-matrices)
- [Reference frames](/egb339/temaer/reference-frames)
- [Pose graphs](/egb339/temaer/pose-graphs)

se-3-homogeneous-transformations.title: SE(3) homogeneous transformations
se-3-homogeneous-transformations.summary: A homogeneous transformation combines orientation and translation:
se-3-homogeneous-transformations.body:
A homogeneous transformation combines orientation and translation:

`T = [[R, t], [0 0 0, 1]]`

where `R ∈ SO(3)` and `t ∈ ℝ³`. A point is written homogeneously as `[x, y, z, 1]ᵀ`.

To check that a matrix belongs to `SE(3)` it must:

- have shape 4×4;
- have bottom row `[0, 0, 0, 1]`;
- contain a valid `SO(3)` matrix in the top-left.

The inverse is

`T⁻¹ = [[Rᵀ, -Rᵀt], [0 0 0, 1]]`.

Ordered multiplication of such matrices is the basis for [Pose graphs](/egb339/temaer/pose-graphs) and [Forward kinematics](/egb339/temaer/forward-kinematics). - [Week 3 - NumPy and 3D pose](/egb339/uker/uke-3)

## Applied frame transformation

In Assessment 2.1, a measured key point expressed in the keyboard's reference frame must be transformed into the robot's base frame before [Inverse kinematics](/egb339/temaer/inverse-kinematics) is used. Homogeneous coordinates turn rotation and translation into a single ordered matrix operation. - [Assessment 2.1 - Simulation and oral demonstration](/egb339/vurderinger/assessment-2-1-simulation-and-oral-demonstration)

See [Keyboard coordinate mapping and safe key presses](/egb339/temaer/keyboard-coordinate-mapping-and-safe-key-presses).

Sources: [Assessment 1.2 - Position and orientation in 3D](/egb339/vurderinger/assessment-1-2-position-and-orientation-in-3d) and [Assessment 2.1 - Simulation and oral demonstration](/egb339/vurderinger/assessment-2-1-simulation-and-oral-demonstration).

shape-descriptors-from-area-and-perimete.title: Shape descriptors from area and perimeter
shape-descriptors-from-area-and-perimete.summary: Area and perimeter can be combined into scale-independent ratios that help distinguish compact shapes such as circles and squares.
shape-descriptors-from-area-and-perimete.body:
> [!abstract] Definition
> Area and perimeter can be combined into scale-independent ratios that help distinguish compact shapes such as circles and squares.

## Useful ratios

- Circle circularity: `C = 4πA/P²`, ideally `C=1` for a perfect circle.
- Square score: `S = 16A/P²`, ideally `S=1` for a perfect square.

> [!tip] Geometric synthesis
> These formulas follow by substituting the exact area and perimeter of a circle or square. Assessment 1.5 asks for classification from area and perimeter and suggests a tolerance, but does not prescribe these exact normalized formulas.

Pixelated boundaries, segmentation noise and imperfect shapes move the score away from its ideal value, so classification needs a tolerance. - [Assessment 1.5 - Warehouse automation](/egb339/vurderinger/assessment-1-5-warehouse-automation)

## Related content

so-2-rotation-matrices.title: SO(2) rotation matrices
so-2-rotation-matrices.summary:
[!definition]
SO(2) is the set of 2×2 matrices that describe pure rotations in the plane.
so-2-rotation-matrices.body:
> [!definition]
> `SO(2)` is the set of `2×2` matrices that describe pure rotations in the plane.

## How it works

For a counter-clockwise rotation `θ`:

`R(θ) = [[cos θ, -sin θ], [sin θ, cos θ]]`

A matrix `R` belongs to `SO(2)` when:

- `R.shape == (2, 2)`;
- `RᵀR = I`;
- `det(R) = +1`.

Orthogonality gives `R⁻¹ = Rᵀ`. The determinant requirement distinguishes a rotation from a reflection. — [Week 2 - Linear algebra and 2D pose](/egb339/uker/uke-2)

## In the EGB339 practicals

Use tolerance in numerical checks: `np.allclose(R.T @ R, np.eye(2))` and `np.isclose(np.linalg.det(R), 1.0)`. This is the direct validation needed in Q2 of [Assessment 1.1 - Position and orientation in 2D](/egb339/vurderinger/assessment-1-1-position-and-orientation-in-2d).

## Related content

so-3-rotation-matrices.title: SO(3) rotation matrices
so-3-rotation-matrices.summary: SO(3) is the set of 3×3 rotation matrices in three dimensions.
so-3-rotation-matrices.body:
`SO(3)` is the set of 3×3 rotation matrices in three dimensions.

A matrix `R` is a valid rotation when:

- `RᵀR = I` (orthogonality)
- `R⁻¹ = Rᵀ`
- `det(R) = +1`

The standard matrices are

`Rx(θ) = [[1,0,0],[0,cosθ,-sinθ],[0,sinθ,cosθ]]`

`Ry(θ) = [[cosθ,0,sinθ],[0,1,0],[-sinθ,0,cosθ]]`

`Rz(θ) = [[cosθ,-sinθ,0],[sinθ,cosθ,0],[0,0,1]]`

Rotations are not commutative: `Rx Ry` is generally different from `Ry Rx`. See [Rotation composition in 3D](/egb339/temaer/rotation-composition-in-3d) and [Reference frames](/egb339/temaer/reference-frames) for interpreting the order and the transformation direction. — [Week 3 - NumPy and 3D pose](/egb339/uker/uke-3)

Source: [Assessment 1.2 - Position and orientation in 3D](/egb339/vurderinger/assessment-1-2-position-and-orientation-in-3d).

trapezoidal-motion-profiles.title: Trapezoidal motion profiles
trapezoidal-motion-profiles.summary: A trapezoidal velocity profile moves through acceleration, constant velocity and deceleration phases so that speed does not change instantaneously.
trapezoidal-motion-profiles.body:
> [!abstract] Definition
> A trapezoidal velocity profile moves through acceleration, constant velocity and deceleration phases so that speed does not change instantaneously.

## Reading the profile

- Displacement equals the area under `v(t)`. - [Week 7 - Motion planning](/egb339/uker/uke-7)
- Acceleration equals the slope `dv/dt`. - [Week 7 - Motion planning](/egb339/uker/uke-7)
- The triangular acceleration and deceleration areas plus the rectangular cruise area must equal the requested travel distance. - [Week 7 - Motion planning](/egb339/uker/uke-7)
- If the move is too short to reach the chosen maximum speed, the profile becomes triangular rather than trapezoidal.

> [!tip] Synthesis
> The triangular short-move case follows from the same area constraint; it is a standard consequence rather than a separately stated Week 7 task.

## Related content

- [Robot motion interpolation](/egb339/temaer/robot-motion-interpolation)
- [Differential kinematics and local linearisation](/egb339/temaer/differential-kinematics-and-local-linearisation)
