assessment-1-problem-solving-task-overvi.body:
> [!abstract] TL;DR
> Assessment 1 is an individual series of autograded coding exercises in robotics, kinematics and computer vision. The whole series counts 20 %, is submitted as the specified Python files on Gradescope and has a limited number of submission attempts before the maximum score is reduced.

## Assessment model

- Assessment 1 counts 20 % and covers fundamental robotics, kinematics and computer vision algorithms.
- Each sub-task provides a code template to be filled in; the implementation is assessed automatically on Gradescope.
- The work is individual, and solutions must not be discussed or shared with other students.
## Submission rules

- The code is submitted electronically on Gradescope by midnight on the due date.
- The tasks are covered by the stated 48-hour period for late submission.
- The first five combined attempts are without penalty. From attempt number six, the highest possible result is reduced by 20 percentage points per further attempt, with a cap of 20 % at nine or more attempts.
> [!warning] Submission strategy
> Run the local public tests and check file names/imports before uploading. Gradescope attempts count collectively per coding task, not per question.

## AI and academic integrity

GenAI may be used to prepare, generate and improve content when the result is critically assessed and the use is acknowledged and referenced according to QUT's rules. The exception applies to the personal oral components that the overall assessment plan mentions for Assessment 2.1 and the later Assessment 2.3.

assessment-1-0-warmup-to-gradescope.body:
> [!abstract] TL;DR
> The warmup is a voluntary 0-point task that trains basic Python, NumPy and the entire submission workflow. All 15 functions must be implemented generally in `assignment1_0.py`, checked with public tests and then tried against Gradescope's hidden private tests.

## Purpose and workflow

- The task is not compulsory, can be completed at any time during the semester and does not count towards the final grade.
- Several questions can be solved in different ways; both a simple programming-language-independent style and a more Pythonic style are allowed as long as the chosen mechanism is understood.
- Run the provided public tests after each question. When they pass, submit `assignment1_0.py` on Gradescope, where hidden private tests check additional cases.
## Question map

| Questions | Skills |
|---|---|
| Q1 | Arithmetic operators and order of parentheses |
| Q2-Q3 | `if`, boolean expressions and compound conditions |
| Q4 | Creating lists and tuples |
| Q5-Q6 | `while` and `for` loops |
| Q7 | Defining a function with arguments and return value |
| Q8-Q10 | NumPy array, `dtype`, `shape` and element-wise arithmetic |
| Q11-Q13 | Transposition, determinant and matrix inverse |
| Q14 | Broadcasting between a `(2,N)` array and column values |
| Q15 | Matrix multiplication of `A B` |

Source: Assessment 1.0 - Warmup to Gradescope.

## General-solution requirement

The example inputs only illustrate certain cases. The functions receive arguments and are tested against private inputs, so the solution must use the arguments and work generally. For Q15, "matrix multiplication of AB" means NumPy matrix multiplication, normally `A @ B`, not element-wise `A * B`.
> [!warning] Source inconsistencies
> The Q15 figure shows `[[12,14],[43,50]]` for the matrices `[[1,2],[3,4]]` and `[[5,6],[7,8]]`, but the correct product `A @ B` is `[[19,22],[43,50]]`. The task text's requirement of matrix multiplication and the function's docstring should be followed. Q3's boundary wording is also unclear; use the starter file's docstring and public tests to confirm the endpoints.

## Key concepts

- [Python control flow and collections](/egb339/temaer/python-control-flow-and-collections)
- [NumPy arrays and matrix operations](/egb339/temaer/numpy-arrays-and-matrix-operations)
- [Linear algebra for robotics](/egb339/temaer/linear-algebra-for-robotics)
- [Public and private autograder tests](/egb339/temaer/public-and-private-autograder-tests)

## Connection to assessment

- Keep the exact required function names, arguments and return types.
- Check `shape` and `dtype`, not only the numerical values.
- Do not hardcode example data; private tests use other valid inputs.
- Use `@` or `np.matmul` for Q15.

assessment-1-1-position-and-orientation-.title: Assessment 1.1 - Position and orientation in 2D
assessment-1-1-position-and-orientation-.summary: Assessment 1.1 tests general functions for SO(2) rotation, validation of rotation matrices, transformation between rotated frames, construction of SE(2) and transformation between rotated and translated frames.
assessment-1-1-position-and-orientation-.body:
> [!abstract] TL;DR
> Assessment 1.1 tests general functions for `SO(2)` rotation, validation of rotation matrices, transformation between rotated frames, construction of `SE(2)` and transformation between rotated and translated frames.

## Requirements

| Question | Required result | Main concept |
|---|---|---|
| Q1 | Compute a `2×2` rotation matrix from an angle in radians | [SO(2) rotation matrices](/egb339/temaer/so-2-rotation-matrices) |
| Q2 | Return `True` only when a NumPy array is a valid `SO(2)` matrix | Orthogonality and determinant `+1` |
| Q3 | Express a point in a new, rotated reference frame | [Reference frames](/egb339/temaer/reference-frames) and transformation direction |
| Q4 | Build a `3×3` homogeneous transformation from a 2D translation and angle | [SE(2) homogeneous transformations](/egb339/temaer/se-2-homogeneous-transformations) |
| Q5 | Transform a homogeneous point between rotated and translated frames | Inverse/composition of `SE(2)` |

The source specifies that the figures only illustrate the situation and do not give the actual parameters of the tests. The functions must therefore solve general input values, not hardcode the examples.
## Frame-direction reasoning

When frame `{B}` is described relative to `{A}`, the direct transformation maps from B coordinates to A coordinates. If the task instead gives a point expressed in A and asks for the B coordinates, the inverse transformation must be used. For a pure rotation, the inverse is the transpose.
## Implementation check

- First check that a candidate matrix has shape `(2,2)`.
- Use `R.T @ R ≈ I` and `det(R) ≈ 1`, with `np.allclose`/`np.isclose`, for `SO(2)`.
- Use `@` for matrix-vector and matrix multiplication; `*` is element-wise multiplication.
- An `SE(2)` matrix has the rotation in the top left, the translation in the last column and bottom row `[0,0,1]`.
- The submission file must be named `assignment1_1.py`; Robotics Toolbox for Python is not allowed.
## Key concepts

- [SO(2) rotation matrices](/egb339/temaer/so-2-rotation-matrices)
- [SE(2) homogeneous transformations](/egb339/temaer/se-2-homogeneous-transformations)
- [Reference frames](/egb339/temaer/reference-frames)
- [NumPy arrays and matrix operations](/egb339/temaer/numpy-arrays-and-matrix-operations)

## Connection to assessment

- Keep the function names and return shapes from the starter file.
- Distinguish between the matrix that describes a frame and the coordinate vector that is to be expressed in another frame.
- Test zero rotation, positive and negative angles, as well as a transformation with both rotation and translation.

assessment-1-2-position-and-orientation-.title: Assessment 1.2 – Position and orientation in 3D
assessment-1-2-position-and-orientation-.summary: The task builds general functions for 3D rotations and homogeneous transformations. It tests both construction, validation and use of SO(3)/SE(3) to express points in different reference frames.
assessment-1-2-position-and-orientation-.body:
> [!abstract] TL;DR
> The task builds general functions for 3D rotations and homogeneous transformations. It tests both construction, validation and use of `SO(3)`/`SE(3)` to express points in different reference frames.

## Academic content

- `rotation_matrix(axis, angle)` must return the correct element in `SO(3)` for the axis `"x"`, `"y"` or `"z"`.
- Composition of rotations is order-dependent and uses matrix multiplication with `@`.
- `transformation_matrix(axis, angle, t)` combines rotation and translation in a `4×4` matrix.
- A valid `SE(3)` matrix has an `SO(3)` rotation block, a three-dimensional translation and bottom row `[0,0,0,1]`.
- `using_so3()` and `using_se3()` test whether transformation direction and reference frame are understood, not only whether the matrix can be constructed.
## Implementation check

- Check the shape before the blocks are indexed.
- Use tolerance-based checks such as `np.allclose` and `np.isclose` for floating-point numbers.
- For the rotation block: `R.T @ R ≈ I` and `det(R) ≈ +1`.
- Return NumPy arrays with the shape that the function's docstring requires.

assessment-1-3-dobot-forward-kinematics.title: Assessment 1.3 – Dobot forward kinematics
assessment-1-3-dobot-forward-kinematics.summary: The task uses an ordered chain of rotations and translations to find the Dobot Magician's end-effector position. It distinguishes four kinematic model angles from the robot's three physical joint angles.
assessment-1-3-dobot-forward-kinematics.body:
> [!abstract] TL;DR
> The task uses an ordered chain of rotations and translations to find the Dobot Magician's end-effector position. It distinguishes four kinematic model angles from the robot's three physical joint angles.

## Workflow

1. Describe the robot's geometry and axes in the home configuration.
2. Build the transformation from base `{0}` to end-effector `{E}` as an ordered product of rotations and translations.
3. Extract the translation part from the final matrix.
4. Connect the robot's three physical joint angles to four kinematic angles in the model.

The Dobot's passive parallel linkage keeps the tool axis vertical. Therefore [Joint-angle mapping](/egb339/temaer/joint-angle-mapping) must handle the difference between the physical and the idealised kinematic model.

## Required interfaces

- `forward_kinematics_q(q)` takes four kinematic angles and returns the end-effector position with shape `(3,)` in millimetres.
- `joint_mapping(theta)` converts three physical angles to the four model angles.
- `forward_kinematics(theta)` must compose the two previous functions instead of duplicating the logic.
## Implementation check

- Use general input values; the example poses in the document are test cases, not hardcoded answers.
- Keep the transformation order from the drawn frame chain.
- Return only the translation column `T[:3, 3]` when the function asks for position.
- Code after a `return` is never reached and should be removed if the starter file's `NotImplementedError` is still there.

## Important links

- [Forward kinematics](/egb339/temaer/forward-kinematics)
- [SE(3) homogeneous transformations](/egb339/temaer/se-3-homogeneous-transformations)
- [Joint-angle mapping](/egb339/temaer/joint-angle-mapping)

assessment-1-4-robot-inverse-kinematics.title: Assessment 1.4 - Robot inverse kinematics
assessment-1-4-robot-inverse-kinematics.summary: The task solves the Dobot's IK in two ways: first by minimising the FK error numerically with scipy.optimize.fmin, then by deriving a fast geometric solution from the top and side views. All results must be verified with Forward kinematics.
assessment-1-4-robot-inverse-kinematics.body:
> [!abstract] TL;DR
> The task solves the Dobot's IK in two ways: first by minimising the FK error numerically with `scipy.optimize.fmin`, then by deriving a fast geometric solution from the top and side views. All results must be verified with [Forward kinematics](/egb339/temaer/forward-kinematics).

## Required model

| Parameter | Value |
|---|---:|
| `L0` | 138 mm |
| `L1` | 135 mm |
| `L2` | 147 mm |
| `L3` | 50 mm |
| `L4` | 120 mm |

These values apply to Assessment 1.4 and must not be mixed with the simulator or physical-robot configuration.
## Tasks

1. Create a cost function that returns the Euclidean distance between the desired target `p*` and `FK(theta)`.
2. Use `scipy.optimize.fmin` to find angles that minimise the cost.
3. Implement geometric IK by solving the top view for `theta1` and the arm plane with distances, the law of cosines and triangle angles.
## Verification

- Use `np.atan2`, not just `np.arctan`, so that the correct quadrant is preserved.
- Insert the computed angles into FK and check that the target point is reconstructed.
- Compare the geometric solution with the optimisation solution.
- The runtime measurement is for your own comparison and is not assessed.
## Key concepts

- [Optimization-based inverse kinematics](/egb339/temaer/optimization-based-inverse-kinematics)
- [Inverse kinematics](/egb339/temaer/inverse-kinematics)
- [atan2 and inverse trigonometry](/egb339/temaer/atan2-and-inverse-trigonometry)
- [Robot workspace and IK solution branches](/egb339/temaer/robot-workspace-and-ik-solution-branches)

## Connection to assessment

- The submission file is `assignment1_4.py`.
- Robotics Toolbox for Python is not allowed in the task.
- The functions must be general for valid targets, not hardcoded to one example.

## Open questions

- How should unreachable targets be signalled without hiding invalid geometry?
- Which IK branch is expected by the hidden tests when multiple solutions exist?

assessment-1-5-warehouse-automation.title: Assessment 1.5 - Warehouse automation
assessment-1-5-warehouse-automation.summary: A pre-segmented warehouse bin provides area and perimeter for each object. The task is to classify the segment as circle, square or other with a general geometric rule and an appropriate tolerance.
assessment-1-5-warehouse-automation.body:
> [!abstract] TL;DR
> A pre-segmented warehouse bin provides area and perimeter for each object. The task is to classify the segment as `circle`, `square` or `other` with a general geometric rule and an appropriate tolerance.

## Problem boundary

The image segmentation and the measurement of area and perimeter have already been performed. The function must only use the two scalar values to decide the shape class.
## Required interface

- Function: `shape_classification(area, perimeter)`
- Input: area in pixels² and perimeter in pixels
- Output: exactly one of the strings `circle`, `square` or `other`
- The task suggests that a tolerance around `0.1` may be useful.
## Key concepts

- [Shape descriptors from area and perimeter](/egb339/temaer/shape-descriptors-from-area-and-perimeter)
- [Digital image representation](/egb339/temaer/digital-image-representation)
- [Image representation and processing](/egb339/temaer/image-representation-and-processing)

## Connection to assessment

- Use a scale-independent relationship between area and perimeter.
- Handle invalid or degenerate measurements so that division by zero is avoided.
- The submission file is `assignment1_5.py`.

## Open questions

- How does pixelation and an uneven segment edge affect the computed perimeter?
- Should the tolerance be applied symmetrically around the ideal shape value?

assessment-1-6-vision-fundamentals-part-.summary: The task counts red, green and blue squares in an RGB image where both base colour and light intensity vary randomly. The solution must therefore separate colour information from total intensity and return the counts in a fixed order.
assessment-1-6-vision-fundamentals-part-.body:
> [!abstract] TL;DR
> The task counts red, green and blue squares in an RGB image where both base colour and light intensity vary randomly. The solution must therefore separate colour information from total intensity and return the counts in a fixed order.

## Required interface

- Function: `coloured_objects(img)`
- Input: an RGB image as `mvt.Image`
- Output: a 3-tuple `(red, green, blue)`
- Gamma correction is not necessary.
## Core challenge

Raw RGB components change when the illumination intensity changes. The classification must use a representation or comparison that preserves the colour relationships better than absolute channel values.
## Key concepts

- [Colour normalization and chromaticity](/egb339/temaer/colour-normalization-and-chromaticity)
- [Digital image representation](/egb339/temaer/digital-image-representation)
- [Image histograms and thresholding](/egb339/temaer/image-histograms-and-thresholding)

## Connection to assessment

- Check the channel order when data comes via OpenCV, which normally reads BGR.
- Use array operations instead of pixel-wise Python loops when possible.
- Test against both light and dark variants of the same base colour.
- The submission file is `assignment1_6.py`.

## Open questions

- How are background pixels distinguished from the coloured squares in the hidden test images?
- How much variation in colour saturation and noise exists in the test data?

assessment-1-7-vision-fundamentals-part-.title: Assessment 1.7 - Vision fundamentals part 2
assessment-1-7-vision-fundamentals-part-.summary: A 3x3 homography connects points on the robot's planar work surface to image points. The task uses the transformation in both directions: image points must be mapped back to the work surface for area calculation, while a work-surface point must be projected into the image.
assessment-1-7-vision-fundamentals-part-.body:
> [!abstract] TL;DR
> A 3x3 homography connects points on the robot's planar work surface to image points. The task uses the transformation in both directions: image points must be mapped back to the work surface for area calculation, while a work-surface point must be projected into the image.

## Mapping convention

The source defines the homography as `p ~ H q`. Here `q` are coordinates on the work surface and `p` are image coordinates. The relation is homogeneous, so the result must be normalised by the third coordinate.
## Tasks

1. Transform the three given image corners back to the work surface and compute the triangle area.
2. Transform a given work-surface point `q` to the image point `p`.
## Key concepts

- [Planar homographies](/egb339/temaer/planar-homographies)
- [Digital image representation](/egb339/temaer/digital-image-representation)
- [Reference frames](/egb339/temaer/reference-frames)

## Connection to assessment

- Keep the transformation direction explicit: `H` goes from work surface to image.
- Add a homogeneous coordinate before multiplication and divide by the last component afterwards.
- Q2 must return a NumPy array with shape `(2, 1)`.
- Q1 returns a scalar area; `cv2.contourArea` is optional.
- The submission file is `assignment1_7.py`.

## Open questions

- How should the code handle a homogeneous result where the scaling component is zero or very small?
- Which numerical tolerance is appropriate when area is computed after a perspective transformation?

assessment-2-applied-project-overview.body:
> [!abstract] TL;DR
> Assessment 2 is an individual project worth 45 % with four parts. Parts 2.1 and 2.2 use kinematics to type words with a simulated and a physical robot arm respectively; parts 2.3 and 2.4 use computer vision for simulated and physical pick-and-place.

## Structure

| Part | Task | Weight | Environment |
|---|---|---:|---|
| [2.1](/egb339/vurderinger/assessment-2-1-simulation-and-oral-demonstration) | Robot word typing | 12.5 % | [CoppeliaSim](/egb339/temaer/coppeliasim) + oral demonstration |

| 2.3 | Vision-guided pick-and-place | 12.5 % | Simulation + oral demonstration |
| 2.4 | Vision-guided pick-and-place | 10 % | Physical robot |

The robotics half transfers one control problem from simulation to hardware, while the computer-vision half repeats the same simulation-to-hardware progression for a perception-guided task.
## Learning outcomes

Assessment 2 measures the ability to recognise realistic robotics and vision problems, implement fundamental algorithms, model and control a multi-link robot arm, and use project-planning techniques.
## Submission and policy signals

- Parts 2.1 and 2.3 require both uploaded code and an in-person oral demonstration; missing the code deadline gives zero for that part.
- Parts 2.2 and 2.4 are code submissions for the physical system and allow the stated 48-hour late period.
- The project is individual, solutions must not be discussed with other students, and any repository used must be private.
- Generative AI may support preparation and refinement, except during the in-person oral components of parts 2.1 and 2.3. AI-generated content must be critically checked, acknowledged and referenced according to QUT guidance.
## Robotics learning path

`keyboard coordinates → [SE(3) homogeneous transformations](/egb339/temaer/se-3-homogeneous-transformations) → [Inverse kinematics](/egb339/temaer/inverse-kinematics) → safe robot motion → simulation validation → physical transfer`

See [Keyboard coordinate mapping and safe key presses](/egb339/temaer/keyboard-coordinate-mapping-and-safe-key-presses), [Robot motion interpolation](/egb339/temaer/robot-motion-interpolation) and [Robot word typing practical](/egb339/ressurser/robot-word-typing-practical).

## Current source coverage

- The current four-page overview confirms all four parts, their weights, the individual-work rule and the AI/oral-demonstration boundary.
- Detailed local task pages are available for the current robotics parts 2.1 and 2.2. Parts 2.3 and 2.4 are only named as later computer-vision parts in the overview; separate pages are not expected among the current files and are not marked as missing.

assessment-2-1-simulation-and-oral-demon.title: Assessment 2.1 - Simulation and oral demonstration
assessment-2-1-simulation-and-oral-demon.summary: Implement a five-letter word-typing controller in CoppeliaSim, upload the code by Sunday 13 September 2026 at 23:59, and demonstrate it individually in the registered Week 9 practical. The core pipeline is keyboard measurement, frame transformation, Inverse kinematics and robot motion; strong solutions also demonstrate joint and Cartesian interpolation.
assessment-2-1-simulation-and-oral-demon.body:
> [!abstract] TL;DR
> Implement a five-letter word-typing controller in [CoppeliaSim](/egb339/temaer/coppeliasim), upload the code by **Sunday 13 September 2026 at 23:59**, and demonstrate it individually in the registered Week 9 practical. The core pipeline is keyboard measurement, frame transformation, [Inverse kinematics](/egb339/temaer/inverse-kinematics) and robot motion; strong solutions also demonstrate joint and Cartesian interpolation.

## Deliverable and demonstration

- The chosen word has five letters; at most one letter may occur twice. Only A-Z keys are required and case does not matter in the simulation.
- The code must be uploaded by the deadline and demonstrated interactively to a practical tutor in Week 9. The 48-hour extension does not apply.
- The demonstration should explain point transformations, key-position handling and IK. The tutor will probe the implementation, mathematics, tests, limitations and results.
- Functional behaviour is worth 2.5 %, while conceptual understanding in the oral questions is worth 10 %.
## Required pipeline

1. Measure the centre of each required key in image pixels relative to a chosen keyboard frame.
2. Scale the measurements to millimetres using the simulated keyboard size of `120 × 290 mm`.
3. Store the key positions in a convenient structure such as a Python dictionary.
4. Determine the homogeneous transform from the keyboard frame to the robot base frame.
5. Transform each key position, solve IK and command the robot to press the key.
This is captured in [Keyboard coordinate mapping and safe key presses](/egb339/temaer/keyboard-coordinate-mapping-and-safe-key-presses) and [Robot word typing practical](/egb339/ressurser/robot-word-typing-practical).

## Simulation configuration

| Parameter | Value |
|---|---:|
| `L0` | 138 mm |
| `L1` | 135 mm |
| `L2` | 147 mm |
| `L3` | 60 mm |
| `L4` | 80 mm |

These parameters reflect the suction-gripper simulation. In the supplied FK expression, the positive `L4` length is applied as a downward offset (subtracted from the vertical coordinate); do not change the stored length to a negative value as well.
## Motion expectations

A working solution must type the selected word. To target the highest functional band, it should additionally demonstrate both joint-interpolated and Cartesian-interpolated motion between letters.
See [Robot motion interpolation](/egb339/temaer/robot-motion-interpolation) and [Differential kinematics and local linearisation](/egb339/temaer/differential-kinematics-and-local-linearisation).

## Oral preparation

Be prepared to explain and test:

- FK from joint angles and the steps in geometric IK;
- the role and extra dimension of homogeneous coordinates;
- additional test cases and unreachable targets;
- how optimisation-based IK could include joint limits or obstacle avoidance;
- execution-time measurement and why it matters;
- how keyboard scaling, such as 75 %, should propagate through the coordinate model.
## Checklist

- [ ] `wordTypingRobot(robotObj, word)` retains the required name and interface.
- [ ] Key coordinates are measured, scaled and stored relative to an explicit keyboard frame.
- [ ] Frame transformation and IK are separated enough to explain independently.
- [ ] Tests cover multiple keys, quadrants, reachability and transformation direction.
- [ ] The submitted code is the same code used in the demonstration.
- [ ] Joint and Cartesian interpolation are demonstrable if aiming for the highest functional band.

assessment-2-2-physical-robot-submission.summary: Port the word-typing solution to the physical Dobot Magician and submit only wordTypingRobot.py by Wednesday 16 September 2026 at 15:59. The robot must type a supplied five-letter lowercase word followed by Enter, while obeying strict height, runtime and API constraints.
assessment-2-2-physical-robot-submission.body:
> [!abstract] TL;DR
> Port the word-typing solution to the physical [Dobot Magician](/egb339/temaer/dobot-magician) and submit only `wordTypingRobot.py` by **Wednesday 16 September 2026 at 15:59**. The robot must type a supplied five-letter lowercase word followed by Enter, while obeying strict height, runtime and API constraints.

## Required interface and behaviour

- Gradescope calls `wordTypingRobot(robotObj, word)` with a Dobot object and a five-letter lowercase word. The controller must type the five letters in order and then press Enter.
- Submit a single file named `wordTypingRobot.py`; remove simulator-specific imports.
- The physical `move_arm(j1, j2, j3)` call is blocking, so `time.sleep()` is unnecessary and must be removed.
- `get_joint_config()` and `get_end_effector_pose()` are unavailable and must not be called.
- Unlike the simulation extension, joint- and Cartesian-interpolated motion must not be used for the physical task.
## Physical geometry

| Item | Physical specification |
|---|---|
| Letter key | 16.2 mm wide × 11.5 mm high |
| Enter key | 19.0 mm wide |
| Keyboard-frame origin in robot frame | `(248, -77.25)` mm |
| Keyboard orientation | 90° about the robot frame's z-axis |
| Kinematic lengths | `L0=138`, `L1=135`, `L2=147`, `L3=60`, `L4=-70` mm |
| Press height | `z=0` mm |
| Minimum lateral-travel height | `z=10` mm |

The physical source lists `L4=-70 mm`, while the current simulation source lists a magnitude `L4=80 mm` that is subtracted in its FK expression. Preserve each source's sign convention instead of comparing the raw signs as if they were defined identically. Every physical quantity is expressed in millimetres.
## Abort conditions

> [!warning] A run is aborted and still counts as a submission if the controller:
> - targets toolbar buttons;
> - commands a point below `z=-5 mm`;
> - moves sideways before lifting the stylus to at least `z=10 mm`;
> - runs longer than one minute; or
> - calls `get_joint_config()` or `get_end_effector_pose()`.
>
> Source: Assessment 2.2 - Physical robot submission.

## Scoring and attempt cost

The score is

`max(0, (10/6)C - min(5, max(0.5(N-1), 0)))`,

where `C` is the number of correct characters in order out of six, including Enter, and `N` is the total number of submissions. Extra or missing characters reduce `C`; repeated submissions add a penalty, and after 11 submissions the maximum possible score is 5/10.
## Transfer checklist

- [ ] Complete and validate [Assessment 2.1 - Simulation and oral demonstration](/egb339/vurderinger/assessment-2-1-simulation-and-oral-demonstration) first.
- [ ] Separate environment-specific constants, especially `L4` and keyboard geometry.
- [ ] Remove simulator imports, unavailable getters, sleeps and interpolation-only demonstration code.
- [ ] Lift to `z≥10 mm` before every sideways move and never command below `z=-5 mm`.
- [ ] Include the Enter key and finish within one minute.
- [ ] Submit only `wordTypingRobot.py` and review the server feedback before another attempt.
